title: The Educated Barbarian: Hagakure analysis (part. 10)
summary: Hagakure commentary: never worship masters, since the path is open to anyone; avoid self-deprecating speech about fear and cowardice; decide quickly; reject contrarian 'misfit' posturing; early talent can be a curse; mindset affects illness; true friends appear in times of need; and act rather than just complain about decline.
claims: Never think a master is unreachable; their achievement is great but the path is accessible to anyone willing to work
Good role models pull you up the mountain hoping you surpass them; those who preach unattainability do it to feed their ego
Very competitive people who hate losing tend to practice more and be more disciplined
Do not say things like 'I am a coward' or 'it hurts'; expressing real emotions like sadness is different and healthy
Modern culture promotes self-deprecation in young men, and some say they would flee a war leaving their parents
Fear and pain happen to you but you can choose not to let them control you, the stoic mindset
Make decisions quickly, within seven breaths
Contrarians who invent oddities to stand out are just reacting to society like teenagers, not being original
However talented, you are of little use if others will not associate with you; you need community
Teaching is its own reward; I have been a teacher for a long time
Early talent can be a curse: gifted people get conceited and by 16-17 hard workers overtake them
I was always strong intellectually but weak physically, and that weakness pushed me to keep improving
People trust those who worked for their achievements because they can teach how they got there
I was sick constantly as a child; since I started training I have not been sick once in 10 years
My grandfather in his 80s still farms daily, butchers pigs and keeps bees, and healed a broken femur in three months against medical expectations
Your mindset during illness matters as much as treatment; sickly people should build a strong mind and body
True friends may not be around in good times but appear without fail when you need them; ditch fair-weather friends
People who see society's decline but only complain are worse than the blind; improve yourself and be a guardian
